title: Loving strangers
hookLine: in several traditions, the stranger is a test of love

lines: THE LAST STRANGER WHO WAS KIND.
WHY THE STRANGER IS A TEST.
cards: Who was the last stranger to do something kind for you? Someone who held a door with a foot while juggling groceries. A driver who waved you into traffic.
A person on a train who pointed out that your bag was open. They may never turn up again, and they didn't need anything back.
Strangers are the people love has the least reason to reach: no history, no debt, no family tie. That's exactly why several ancient texts made the stranger a test.

teach.b: First, Abraham runs to the strangers. In Genesis, Abraham is sitting at the door of his tent in the heat of the day when he sees three men standing nearby. He doesn't wait to find out who they are.
He runs to meet them, bows, and asks them to stay. Then he hurries: water for their feet, fresh bread, a calf prepared, food set before them while he stands by.
The chapter opens by telling the reader that the LORD appeared to Abraham there; how much Abraham himself understood at first, the text leaves open.
Second, ye were strangers. Leviticus doesn't just say tolerate the outsider: "thou shalt love him as thyself; for ye were strangers in the land of Egypt." The reason given is memory.
You know what it's like to be the outsider.
Third, angels unawares. The letter to the Hebrews has a line in which some readers hear Abraham's story: "Be not forgetful to entertain strangers: for thereby some have entertained angels unawares."
The Greeks had their own version: in Homer's Odyssey, a princess tells her frightened friends that strangers and beggars come from Zeus.

Fourth, a smile is small hospitality. Not everyone has a tent or a calf to offer. But hospitality comes in small sizes: eye contact with the cashier, patience with a lost tourist, a nod to the new person at work.
These texts treat the stranger not as a risk to manage but as someone to welcome, with common sense about safety. Here, the stranger is where love reaches past loyalty.

how: Jews and Christians read Abraham's welcome of three guests in Genesis 18 as a model of hospitality, and the Torah commands love for the stranger; hospitality to guests and travelers is also honored in other faiths and cultures.

o: welcome for people who have no claim on you
tolerating outsiders as long as they stay away
kindness kept only for guests you already know

games.q: who welcomed the stranger — tap the pairs.
p: for ye were strangers in Egypt

s: in Genesis, Abraham waits at his tent for the three men to come to him
he runs from the tent door to meet them, bows, and asks them to stay.
Leviticus gives a reason for loving the stranger: ye were strangers in Egypt
the command is grounded in memory.
Hebrews says hospitality to strangers is optional for the wise
be not forgetful to entertain strangers.

games.q: you're Abraham, resting at your tent in the heat. three men you've never seen appear nearby. what do you do?
o: stay seated and watch them warily.
run to meet them and ask them to stay.
send someone to ask what they want.
games.why: Abraham runs, bows, and hurries to bring water, bread and a meal. the chapter opens by saying the LORD appeared to him there.

practice: Let a stranger who once did something kind for you come back to mind, a door held, a wave into traffic, directions on a strange street, and stay with that moment for a few breaths.
Let the thanks you never got to say be said silently now. If you pray, you can give thanks for that stranger before God, nameless as they are.

wordCard.voice: Loving strangers. Welcome offered to people with no claim on you, the way Abraham ran to his guests and Leviticus says to love the outsider as yourself. Today's word.

orig.note: philoxenia, the Greek word behind 'entertain strangers' in Hebrews 13:2.

carryVoice: Your line: the stranger. Every one of us has been the outsider somewhere. Until tomorrow.
